questions.q: Before generating a new project, what two things does this lab's Step 1 say you should confirm?
options: That you have a GitHub account and a VS Code installation
That a namespace has already been registered
That a scratch org already exists
That the CLI reports the current @salesforce/cli/2.x version, and that your Dev Hub shows up as the default Dev Hub in sf org list
questions.explain: Step 1 confirms your tooling is actually ready before anything else: sf version should report the current CLI generation, and sf org list should show your Dev Hub as the default — everything downstream depends on both being correct.

questions.q: Which command does Step 2 use to scaffold the new project's standard folder structure?
options: sf project generate --name dx-capstone
sf org create scratch
sf package create
sf project deploy start
questions.explain: sf project generate --name dx-capstone scaffolds the standard Salesforce DX project structure that the rest of the lab builds on, matching the project structure covered in Lesson 7.

questions.q: In Step 3, what value should `namespace` be set to in sfdx-project.json for this particular lab project?
options: A newly registered production namespace
"Unlocked"
Empty — this project isn't registering a namespace or building a package in this lab
The Dev Hub's org ID
questions.explain: This lab leaves namespace empty, since the project isn't registering a namespace or building a package here — namespaces matter specifically for packaging work covered in Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why does Step 5 add a real Apex class to the project before moving on to Lesson 20?
options: Apex classes are required for sf project generate to succeed
To give Lesson 20's deploy lab an actual component to push into a scratch org, rather than an empty project
Because sfdx-project.json requires at least one Apex class to be valid
Apex classes are required before a scratch org definition file can be written
questions.explain: Step 5 exists specifically so there's real, concrete metadata to deploy in the next lesson — an empty project wouldn't give Lesson 20's deploy exercise anything meaningful to push.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say committing to Git (Step 6) is the step that actually makes the project "source-driven"?
options: Because Git automatically creates a scratch org
Because Git uploads the files directly to the Dev Hub
Because sfdx-project.json requires a Git repository to parse correctly
Because it's the point at which the local files become the project's authoritative, version-controlled source of truth, matching the source-driven model from Lesson 3
questions.explain: Per Lesson 3's source-driven development model, the local file system becomes the authoritative source of truth once it's committed to version control — before that commit, it's just a folder of generated files with no tracked history.
